title: Telugu's Funniest Married Men Are Back. Save the Tigers 3 Adds a God to the Mess.
excerpt: JioHotstar's beloved marital comedy returns June 19 with a fantasy twist — Vennela Kishore as Lord Indra — and three husbands whose complaints keep accidentally making headlines.
body:
If you have ever sat in a Telugu household and watched three grown men commiserate about their marriages with the gravity of war veterans, you already understand the appeal of **Save the Tigers**. The web series that turned domestic griping into an art form is back for a third season, and it lands on **JioHotstar on June 19** — perfectly timed for a diaspora weekend binge.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=wob0NDMQqGY</youtube>

Here is what the franchise has always understood: the funniest comedy isn't found in elaborate setpieces, it's in the everyday absurdity of marriage, in-laws, and the quiet desperation of men who love their wives but would also very much like to win one argument, just once. Across two seasons, the misadventures of its central trio — three husbands navigating the minefield of married life — built a loyal following precisely because the chaos felt familiar. You weren't laughing *at* them. You were laughing because you, or your uncle, or your father, were them.

Season 3, directed by **Arun Kothapally**, throws a delicious wrench into the formula. This time there's a fantasy twist, and the agent of chaos is none other than **Vennela Kishore** joining the cast as **Lord Indra** — yes, the king of the gods himself, descending into the very mortal mess of suburban marriage. If you know Vennela Kishore's comic timing, the casting alone is worth the price of admission. The man can wring a laugh out of a raised eyebrow, and handing him a divine role in a show about henpecked husbands is the kind of inspired absurdity that makes Telugu OTT comedy so reliably good right now.

The returning ensemble brings back the chemistry that made the show click — **Priyadarshi**, Jordaar Sujatha, Chaitanya Krishna, Abhinav Gomatam, and the rest of the gang whose group dynamic carries the series. Priyadarshi, in particular, has quietly become one of the most dependable comic presences in Telugu cinema, the kind of actor who elevates every scene he's dropped into. The premise this season leans into a sharp, modern gag: the husbands' very public complaints about their marital woes unexpectedly start making headlines, turning private grievance into accidental fame.

> The three husbands' public complaints about their marital lives unexpectedly make headlines — and the chaos writes itself.

What makes *Save the Tigers* such a smart watch is that it never punches down. The wives aren't villains and the husbands aren't heroes; everybody is a little ridiculous, everybody is a little right, and the comedy comes from the collision. It's *Modern Family* energy filtered through a distinctly Telugu sensibility, and the addition of a mythological layer this season suggests the writers are willing to push the show somewhere stranger and bolder.

For the diaspora, the where-to-watch is refreshingly simple. **Save the Tigers Season 3 streams on JioHotstar from June 19**, which means subscribers across the US, UK, and Canada — where JioHotstar (via its international apps) carries the bulk of Telugu OTT originals — can stream it day-and-date with India. No waiting, no piracy guilt, no hunting for a working link at 2 a.m. The series is in Telugu, and JioHotstar typically offers subtitles, making it accessible even to the second-gen kids whose Telugu is more *understood* than *spoken*.

It arrives in a stacked week, too. June 19 is shaping up to be a genuine traffic jam of releases — Drishyam 3 hit Prime Video the day before, Cocktail 2 storms theatres, and Netflix is triple-dropping. But there's a specific comfort to a show like *Save the Tigers*: it doesn't demand your full attention, it doesn't ask you to keep track of a labyrinthine plot, it just wants to make you laugh at the gentle warfare of married life. For an NRI audience juggling time zones, jobs, and the eternal long-distance negotiation with relatives back home, that low-stakes, high-warmth comedy is exactly the kind of thing that goes down easy on a Friday night.

Three seasons in, the show knows precisely what it is. Add a god to the chaos, and you've got a recipe for the most entertaining marital meltdown of the summer.
